Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Loss on issue when Securities Premium is insufficient
questions.question: Apex Ltd. issued 3,000, 10% debentures of ₹100 each at a premium of 5%, redeemable at a premium of 10%. The company had no other balance in Securities Premium. When the loss on issue of debentures is written off in the year of issue, the amount charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹15,000
Step 1: Premium on issue credited to Securities Premium = 3,000 × ₹5 = ₹15,000
Step 2: Loss on issue (premium payable on redemption) = 3,000 × ₹10 = ₹30,000
Step 3: Write-off: ₹15,000 from Securities Premium; the balance of ₹15,000 from the Statement of Profit and Loss
Common mistake: Charging the whole loss to P&L gives ₹30,000 (A). Assuming the premium covers it gives Nil (C). Adding the premium and the loss gives ₹45,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Section 37 — rights of an outgoing partner
questions.question: Harsh retired from a firm, but the continuing partners carried on the business without settling his account. Under Section 37 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, Harsh is entitled, at his option, to:
options: A) Interest at 12% p.a. on the amount due
C) A share of the profits only
D) Either interest at 6% p.a. on the amount due, or the share of profits earned by the use of his share of the firm's property
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Either interest at 6% p.a. on the amount due, or the share of profits earned by the use of his share of the firm's property
Why: Section 37 gives the outgoing partner (or his legal representative) the CHOICE between these two amounts until the account is settled.
Why not the others: (A) The rate is 6%, not 12%. (B) and (C) each state only one half of the option.
Key point: Section 37 = a choice between 6% interest and the attributable profit.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Rules applicable in the absence of a partnership deed
questions.question:
Neel and Omar run a business without any partnership deed. Which of the following statements apply to them?
(A) Neither of them is entitled to a salary.
(B) A loan given by Neel to the firm will carry interest at 6% p.a.
(C) Each of them will get interest on capital at 6% p.a.
(D) No interest will be charged on their drawings.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: Under Section 13 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, when there is no agreement: no partner gets a salary (A); a partner's loan carries interest at 6% p.a. (B); and no interest is charged on drawings (D).
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — without an agreement, NO interest on capital is allowed. The 6% rate applies only to loans. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Deed silent → equal profit share, 6% on loans only, nothing else.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Balance sheet — share capital with arrears and forfeited shares
questions.question: Crest Ltd. issued 60,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, of which 50,000 were subscribed, and ₹8 per share has been called up. Of the subscribed shares, 1,000 shares (on which ₹6 per share had been paid) were forfeited and not re-issued. On the remaining shares, calls in arrears are ₹4,000. The total share capital shown in the balance sheet is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹3,94,000
Step 1: Subscribed but not fully paid = 49,000 × ₹8 = ₹3,92,000, less calls in arrears ₹4,000 = ₹3,88,000
Step 2: Add forfeited shares account (1,000 × ₹6) = ₹6,000
Step 3: Total = ₹3,94,000
Common mistake: 50,000 × ₹8 gives ₹4,00,000 (A). Deducting only the arrears from it gives ₹3,96,000 (B). Leaving out the forfeited amount gives ₹3,88,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Debentures — redemption premium, loss on issue and interest
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about debentures:
(A) Debentures may be issued at a discount.
(B) Premium payable on redemption is a liability of the company until the debentures are redeemed.
(C) Loss on issue of debentures is written off first from Securities Premium, if a balance is available.
(D) Interest on debentures is an appropriation of profit.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Debentures can be issued at a discount (A). The premium promised on redemption must be paid later, so it is a liability (B). Loss on issue is written off from Securities Premium first and then from the Statement of Profit and Loss (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — debenture interest is a CHARGE (finance cost), payable even in a loss year. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Debenture interest = charge; dividend = appropriation.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Shares issued at a premium — amount of the final call
questions.question: Shares of ₹10 each are issued at a premium of ₹2. The amount payable is ₹3 on application and ₹5 on allotment (including the premium), with the balance on the first and final call. The amount of the first and final call per share is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹4
Step 1: Total payable per share = ₹10 + ₹2 = ₹12
Step 2: Paid on application and allotment = ₹3 + ₹5 = ₹8
Step 3: Call = ₹12 − ₹8 = ₹4 (all towards share capital, since the premium was collected with allotment)
Common mistake: Ignoring the premium altogether gives ₹2 (B). Ignoring the application money gives ₹7 (C). Ignoring the allotment money gives ₹9 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Journal entries in share capital transactions
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Transaction)
(A) Receipt of application money
(B) Transfer of application money on allotment
(C) Forfeiture of shares
(D) Transfer of the gain on forfeited shares that have been re-issued

List-II (Entry)
(I) Bank A/c Dr.; To Share Application A/c
(II) Share Application A/c Dr.; To Share Capital A/c
(III) Share Capital A/c Dr.; To Share Forfeiture A/c and To the unpaid Allotment/Call A/cs
(IV) Share Forfeiture A/c Dr.; To Capital Reserve A/c
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Money received is credited to Share Application (I).
(B) On allotment it becomes share capital (II).
(C) Forfeiture cancels the called-up capital, credits the amount received to Share Forfeiture and closes the unpaid calls (III).
(D) After re-issue, the surplus is a capital profit → Capital Reserve (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps receipt and transfer; (C) swaps transfer and forfeiture; (D) swaps forfeiture and capital reserve.
Key point: Follow the life of a share: apply → allot → forfeit → re-issue.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: New partner's capital proportionate to old partners' capital
questions.question: After all adjustments, Amar and Bela have capitals of ₹2,40,000 and ₹1,60,000. Chand is admitted for a 1/5th share, and his capital is to be proportionate to his share, based on the combined capital of Amar and Bela. Chand's capital is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,00,000
Step 1: Old partners together hold 4/5, with capital ₹4,00,000
Step 2: Total capital of the new firm = ₹4,00,000 × 5/4 = ₹5,00,000
Step 3: Chand's capital = ₹5,00,000 × 1/5 = ₹1,00,000
Common mistake: Taking 1/5 of ₹4,00,000 gives ₹80,000 (A). ₹1,25,000 (B) and ₹2,00,000 (C) do not follow the proportion.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: New partner's share from fractions surrendered by old partners
questions.question: Arun and Bala share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. Arun surrenders 1/3 of his share and Bala surrenders 1/4 of her share in favour of a new partner, Chetna. Chetna's share of profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3/10
Step 1: From Arun = 1/3 × 3/5 = 1/5
Step 2: From Bala = 1/4 × 2/5 = 1/10
Step 3: Chetna = 1/5 + 1/10 = 3/10
Common mistake: Adding the fractions directly (1/3 + 1/4) gives 7/12 (B). 1/5 (C) is only Arun's contribution. 1/10 (D) is only Bala's.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Premium on redemption of debentures — account credited
questions.question: Kirti Ltd. issues debentures at their face value but promises to repay them at 105. Which account records this promise to pay the extra ₹5 per debenture?
options: B) Statement of Profit and Loss
D) Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c
Why: The premium is a future liability. It is credited to the Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c (shown under non-current liabilities), while the matching Loss on Issue of Debentures A/c is debited.
Why not the others:
(A) Securities Premium is credited only for premium received on ISSUE.
(B) and (C) are not used for this liability.
Key point: Premium received on issue → Securities Premium; premium payable on redemption → a liability account.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Need for valuing goodwill on admission
questions.question: Goodwill is valued at the time of admitting a new partner mainly because:
options: A) The old partners give up part of their future profits, and the new partner compensates them for it
B) The law requires every firm to show goodwill in its balance sheet
C) Goodwill is a current asset that must be revalued every year
D) The new partner brings capital into the firm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The old partners give up part of their future profits, and the new partner compensates them for it
Why: The firm's reputation was built by the old partners. When a new partner takes a share of future profits, the old partners sacrifice, so goodwill is valued to fix their compensation.
Why not the others: (B) There is no such legal requirement. (C) Goodwill is not a current asset. (D) Capital contribution is a separate matter.
Key point: Sacrifice of future profit → compensation through goodwill.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Cash received on allotment with pro-rata adjustment and default
questions.question: A company received applications for 25,000 shares against 20,000 shares offered and allotted pro rata to all applicants. Application money was ₹2 and allotment money ₹4 per share, and excess application money was adjusted against allotment. Mohit, who had applied for 500 shares, failed to pay the allotment money. The cash received on allotment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹68,600
Step 1: Allotment due = 20,000 × ₹4 = ₹80,000; excess application = 5,000 × ₹2 = ₹10,000 → net due ₹70,000
Step 2: Mohit was allotted 400 shares; his allotment = ₹1,600, less his excess application (100 × ₹2 = ₹200) → unpaid ₹1,400
Step 3: Cash received = ₹70,000 − ₹1,400 = ₹68,600
Common mistake: Assuming full payment gives ₹70,000 (A). Ignoring the adjustment gives ₹78,400 (C). Deducting Mohit's full ₹1,600 gives ₹68,400 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share capital — authorised capital
questions.question: The maximum amount of share capital that a company is permitted to raise, as stated in the capital clause of its Memorandum of Association, is its:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Authorised capital
Why: Authorised (or nominal/registered) capital is the ceiling fixed by the Memorandum. The company cannot issue shares beyond it without altering the Memorandum.
Why not the others:
(A) Issued capital is the part offered to the public.
(C) Subscribed capital is the part taken up.
(D) Called-up capital is the part demanded.
Key point: Authorised ≥ Issued ≥ Subscribed ≥ Called-up ≥ Paid-up.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings — equal amounts in the middle of every month
questions.question: Throughout 2025-26, Sameer drew ₹4,000 from the firm in the middle of every month. The deed charges interest on drawings at 9% p.a. How much interest on drawings will be debited to Sameer's account at the end of the year?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹2,160
Given: Total drawings = 12 × ₹4,000 = ₹48,000, drawn in the middle of each month.
Step 1: Average period for mid-month drawings = 6 months
Step 2: Interest = ₹48,000 × 9% × 6/12 = ₹2,160
Common mistake: Using 5.5 months (end of month) gives ₹1,980 (A). Using 6.5 months (beginning of month) gives ₹2,340 (B). Charging a full year gives ₹4,320 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — hidden goodwill from the settlement amount
questions.question: Ajay, Bhanu and Chandni share profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. Chandni retires and is paid ₹70,000 in full settlement. Her capital, after crediting her share of reserves and revaluation profit, was ₹55,000. Goodwill does not appear in the books, and Ajay and Bhanu will share future profits equally. The amount debited to Ajay's Capital Account for goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹7,500
Step 1: Excess paid = ₹70,000 − ₹55,000 = ₹15,000 → Chandni's share of goodwill
Step 2: Firm's goodwill = ₹15,000 × 5 = ₹75,000
Step 3: Gains: Ajay = 1/2 − 2/5 = 1/10; Bhanu = 1/2 − 2/5 = 1/10 → gaining ratio 1 : 1
Step 4: Ajay's debit = ₹15,000 × 1/2 = ₹7,500
Common mistake: Charging Ajay the whole ₹15,000 gives (B). Half of the firm's goodwill gives ₹37,500 (C). Using 2/5 of ₹15,000 gives ₹6,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Premium for goodwill — sharing among old partners
questions.question:
Assertion (A): The premium for goodwill brought in cash by a new partner is shared by the old partners in their sacrificing ratio.
Reason (R): The premium is the new partner's compensation to the old partners for the share of future profits they give up.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Since the premium is paid as compensation for sacrifice (R), it must go to those who sacrifice, in the proportion of their sacrifice — the sacrificing ratio (A).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason directly explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Who sacrifices, receives — in the sacrificing ratio.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Securities Premium — not available for dividend
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A company cannot use its Securities Premium to pay a dividend to its shareholders.
Reason (R): Securities Premium is a capital receipt, and Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013 restricts its use to specified purposes.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Because Securities Premium is a capital receipt, Section 52 limits its use to purposes such as issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses or the discount/expenses on issue of securities, providing for the premium on redemption, and buy-back. Dividend is not among them — which is exactly why the Assertion holds.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason is the explanation. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Securities Premium = capital profit; dividends come from revenue profits.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue of forfeited shares as partly paid
questions.question: Pinnacle Ltd. forfeited 200 shares of ₹10 each (₹8 called up: application ₹2, allotment ₹3, first call ₹3) because the holder paid only the application money. All 200 shares were later re-issued as ₹8 paid-up for ₹6 per share. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Nil
Step 1: Amount forfeited = 200 × ₹2 = ₹400
Step 2: The shares are re-issued as ₹8 paid-up for ₹6 → discount = 200 × ₹2 = ₹400
Step 3: Balance in Share Forfeiture = ₹400 − ₹400 = Nil → nothing to transfer
Common mistake: Ignoring the discount gives ₹400 (A). ₹1,200 (B) is the cash received on re-issue. Treating the holder as having paid ₹5 per share gives ₹600 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in profit-sharing ratio — goodwill adjustment
questions.question: Ira, Jai and Kim share profits equally. From 1 April 2026 they decide to share in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹90,000, and it is not to be shown in the books. The adjusting entry is:
options: A) Kim's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Ira's Capital A/c ₹15,000
B) Ira's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Kim's Capital A/c ₹15,000
C) Ira's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Jai's and Kim's Capital A/cs ₹7,500 each
D) Ira's Capital A/c Dr. ₹30,000; To Kim's Capital A/c ₹30,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ira's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Kim's Capital A/c ₹15,000
Step 1: Old share of each = 2/6
Step 2: Ira gains 3/6 − 2/6 = 1/6; Jai's share is unchanged (2/6); Kim sacrifices 2/6 − 1/6 = 1/6
Step 3: Amount = ₹90,000 × 1/6 = ₹15,000, paid by Ira to Kim
Common mistake: Reversing the entry gives (A). Treating Jai as sacrificing gives (C). Using 2/6 instead of 1/6 gives ₹30,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — super profit with an abnormal loss
questions.question: A firm's profits for four years were: 2022-23 ₹70,000; 2023-24 ₹60,000 (after an abnormal loss of ₹20,000 from a fire); 2024-25 ₹90,000; 2025-26 ₹80,000. Capital employed is ₹5,00,000 and the normal rate of return is 10%. Goodwill is valued at three years' purchase of super profit. Its value is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹90,000
Step 1: Normal profit of 2023-24 = ₹60,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹80,000 (the abnormal loss is added back)
Step 2: Average profit = (70,000 + 80,000 + 90,000 + 80,000) ÷ 4 = ₹80,000
Step 3: Normal profit = 10% × ₹5,00,000 = ₹50,000
Step 4: Super profit = ₹30,000; Goodwill = ₹30,000 × 3 = ₹90,000
Common mistake: Not adding back the abnormal loss (average ₹75,000) gives ₹75,000 (A). ₹30,000 (C) is the super profit. Three years' purchase of the average profit gives ₹2,40,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Debentures — unsecured
questions.question: Debentures that do not carry any charge on the company's assets are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Unsecured (naked) debentures
Why: Unsecured debentures depend only on the company's general credit; holders rank with other unsecured creditors.
Why not the others:
(A) Collateral debentures are given as extra security for a loan.
(B) Registered refers to how holders are recorded.
(C) Convertible refers to the right to convert into shares.
Key point: Security → secured or unsecured; records → registered or bearer; conversion → convertible or non-convertible.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Interest on debentures issued during the year
questions.question: Orion Ltd. issued 12% debentures of ₹5,00,000 on 1 July 2025. How much debenture interest should appear as finance cost in its Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ending 31 March 2026?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹45,000
Step 1: Period from 1 July 2025 to 31 March 2026 = 9 months
Step 2: Interest = ₹5,00,000 × 12% × 9/12 = ₹45,000
Common mistake: A full year gives ₹60,000 (A). 6 months gives ₹30,000 (B). 3 months gives ₹15,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Creditor accepting an asset at a discount in part settlement
questions.question: On dissolution, creditors of ₹50,000 agreed to take over stock (book value ₹46,000, already transferred to the Realisation Account) at 10% less than its book value, and to receive the balance in cash. The cash paid to the creditors is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹8,600
Step 1: Value at which the stock is accepted = ₹46,000 − 10% = ₹41,400
Step 2: Cash balance payable = ₹50,000 − ₹41,400 = ₹8,600 (Realisation A/c Dr.; To Cash A/c)
Common mistake: Using the book value of stock gives ₹4,000 (A). Ignoring the stock gives ₹50,000 (C). Taking 10% of the creditors gives ₹5,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Dissolution expenses paid by the firm
questions.question: On dissolution, the firm paid realisation expenses of ₹4,000. The entry is:
options: A) Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. ₹4,000; To Cash A/c ₹4,000
B) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To Partner's Capital A/c ₹4,000
C) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To Cash A/c ₹4,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To Cash A/c ₹4,000
Why: Expenses borne and paid by the firm are a cost of realisation, so they are debited to the Realisation Account and reduce the profit (or increase the loss).
Why not the others:
(A) Capitals are affected only through the final realisation result.
(B) is the entry when a PARTNER pays the expenses on the firm's behalf.
(D) A cash payment must be recorded.
Key point: Firm pays → Realisation Dr.; To Cash.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — amount payable to the executor
questions.question: Dev, a partner with a 1/4th share, died on 30 September 2026. His capital on 1 April 2026 was ₹80,000, and his drawings up to the date of death were ₹5,000. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. His share of profit up to the date of death is to be based on the previous year's profit of ₹1,20,000, and interest on capital is allowed at 10% p.a. The amount payable to his executor is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,24,000
Step 1: Share of goodwill = ₹1,20,000 × 1/4 = ₹30,000
Step 2: Profit for 6 months (1 April–30 September) = ₹1,20,000 × 6/12 × 1/4 = ₹15,000
Step 3: Interest on capital for 6 months = ₹80,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹4,000
Step 4: Amount payable = 80,000 + 30,000 + 15,000 + 4,000 − 5,000 = ₹1,24,000
Common mistake: Not deducting drawings gives ₹1,29,000 (A). Ignoring goodwill gives ₹94,000 (B). Ignoring his profit share gives ₹1,09,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation loss with several realisation items
questions.question: On dissolution, the firm's assets (other than cash) were stock ₹50,000, debtors ₹60,000 and machinery ₹90,000. Stock was sold at 10% below book value; debtors realised 95%; partner Asif took over the machinery at ₹80,000; an unrecorded investment was sold for ₹5,000; creditors of ₹40,000 were paid at a 2% discount; and realisation expenses were ₹3,000. The loss on realisation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹15,200
Step 1: Stock −₹5,000; debtors −₹3,000; machinery −₹10,000 → loss on assets ₹18,000
Step 2: Unrecorded investment +₹5,000
Step 3: Discount on creditors (2% × ₹40,000) +₹800
Step 4: Expenses −₹3,000
Step 5: Net = −18,000 + 5,000 + 800 − 3,000 = −₹15,200 (loss)
Common mistake: Ignoring the unrecorded investment gives ₹20,200 (A). Ignoring the creditors' discount gives ₹16,000 (B). Ignoring the expenses gives ₹12,200 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Factors affecting goodwill
questions.question:
Which of the following statements about the factors affecting goodwill are correct?
(A) A favourable location increases goodwill.
(B) Efficient management increases goodwill.
(C) Monopoly or limited competition increases goodwill.
(D) A firm that earns less than the normal rate of return on its capital has high goodwill.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: A good location attracts customers (A), efficient management raises profits (B), and limited competition allows above-normal earnings (C) — all of these increase goodwill.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — goodwill comes from earning MORE than the normal return. A firm earning below normal has no goodwill. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Goodwill = capacity to earn super profits.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Revaluation Account — purpose
questions.question: At the time of a partner's admission, the increases and decreases in the values of assets and liabilities are recorded in the:
options: B) Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Revaluation Account
Why: The Revaluation Account (also called the Profit and Loss Adjustment Account) records the revised values, and its net profit or loss is transferred to the old partners.
Why not the others:
(A) The Realisation Account is used on dissolution.
(B) The Appropriation Account distributes the year's profit.
(C) Current Accounts receive only the final result.
Key point: Reconstitution → Revaluation A/c; dissolution → Realisation A/c.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Definition of partnership — section
questions.question: 'Partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.' This definition is given in which section of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Section 4
Why: Section 4 defines partnership and brings out its essentials — an agreement, a business, sharing of profits and mutual agency.
Why not the others:
(B) Section 13 covers rights of partners where the deed is silent.
(C) Section 37 covers an outgoing partner's right to subsequent profits or interest.
(D) Section 48 covers the settlement of accounts on dissolution.
Key point: Section 4 → definition; Section 13 → default rules; Section 48 → dissolution.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Dissolution — order of accounting steps
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps in closing the books of a dissolved firm in the correct order:
(A) Pay the final balances of the partners' Capital Accounts
(B) Transfer the profit or loss on realisation to the partners' Capital Accounts
(C) Transfer the assets and outside liabilities to the Realisation Account
(D) Record the sale of assets and the payment of liabilities
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C), (D), (B), (A)
Why: Book values are first transferred to the Realisation Account (C). The amounts actually realised and paid are then recorded (D). Only then is the profit or loss known and transferred to the capitals (B), after which the final balances are settled in cash (A).
Why not the others: (B) records sales before the accounts are transferred. (C) finds the result before sales are recorded. (D) pays the partners first.
Key point: Transfer → realise → result → settle.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: New ratio when the new partner takes specified fractions from each partner
questions.question: Arun and Bala share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. Chris is admitted for a 1/4th share, which he takes 1/6 from Arun and 1/12 from Bala. What will be the profit-sharing ratio of the reconstituted firm?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 26 : 19 : 15
Step 1: Arun = 3/5 − 1/6 = 18/30 − 5/30 = 13/30 = 26/60
Step 2: Bala = 2/5 − 1/12 = 24/60 − 5/60 = 19/60
Step 3: Chris = 1/4 = 15/60
Step 4: New ratio = 26 : 19 : 15
Common mistake: 9 : 6 : 5 (A) assumes sacrifice in the old ratio. 3 : 2 : 1 (B) has no basis. 13 : 19 : 15 (D) mixes denominators of 30 and 60.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Journal entry for making a call
questions.question: When the directors make the first call on shares, the entry for the amount due is:
options: A) Bank A/c Dr.; To Share First Call A/c
B) Share Capital A/c Dr.; To Share First Call A/c
C) Share First Call A/c Dr.; To Bank A/c
D) Share First Call A/c Dr.; To Share Capital A/c
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Share First Call A/c Dr.; To Share Capital A/c
Why: Making the call converts that amount into called-up capital and creates an amount receivable from shareholders, recorded in the First Call A/c.
Why not the others:
(A) is the entry when the call money is RECEIVED.
(B) reverses the correct entry.
(C) would mean the company pays money out.
Key point: Call made → Call A/c Dr.; To Share Capital. Money received → Bank Dr.; To Call A/c.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — treatment of items
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II on the retirement of a partner:

List-I (Item)
(A) Retiring partner's share of profit up to the date of retirement
(B) Amount due to the retiring partner that is not paid immediately
(C) Profit on revaluation
(D) Retiring partner's share of goodwill

List-II (Treatment)
(I) Debited to the continuing partners in their gaining ratio
(II) Profit and Loss Suspense A/c Dr.; To Retiring Partner's Capital A/c
(III) Credited to all the partners in their old ratio
(IV) Transferred to the retiring partner's Loan Account
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why:
(A) Profit to the date of retirement is credited to him through P&L Suspense (II).
(B) An unpaid balance becomes a loan to the firm (IV).
(C) Revaluation profit belongs to all the partners in the old ratio (III).
(D) The gaining partners compensate him for goodwill (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the profit and goodwill entries; (B) swaps the loan and revaluation; (D) swaps the profit and loan entries.
Key point: Old ratio for past gains; gaining ratio for goodwill.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Revaluation profit with a new provision and creditors written back
questions.question: On the admission of a partner: the building is to be appreciated by ₹30,000; stock is to be reduced by ₹8,000; a provision for doubtful debts at 5% is to be created on debtors of ₹60,000; and creditors include ₹2,000 that will not have to be paid. The profit on revaluation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹21,000
Step 1: Gains — building +₹30,000; creditors written back +₹2,000
Step 2: Losses — stock −₹8,000; provision (5% × ₹60,000) −₹3,000
Step 3: Profit = 30,000 + 2,000 − 8,000 − 3,000 = ₹21,000
Common mistake: Treating the creditors written back as a loss gives ₹17,000 (A). Ignoring the provision gives ₹24,000 (C). Ignoring the fall in stock gives ₹29,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Dissolution of partnership versus dissolution of firm
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Dissolution of a firm necessarily involves dissolution of the partnership.
(B) Dissolution of a partnership necessarily ends the business of the firm.
(C) When only the partnership is dissolved, the books of the firm are not closed.
(D) A court may order the dissolution of a firm.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: When a firm is dissolved, the relationship among all partners ends, so the partnership ends too (A). When only the partnership is reconstituted, the firm continues and the books are not closed (C). Section 44 allows the court to dissolve a firm (D).
Why not the others: Statement (B) is false — after an admission, retirement or death, the business usually continues under a new agreement. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Firm dissolved → business ends; partnership dissolved → business may continue.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — omitted interest on capital
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Pallavi, Qadir and Rohan are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Their capitals are fixed at ₹3,00,000, ₹2,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. The firm's profit of ₹1,80,000 for 2025-26 was distributed among them in their profit-sharing ratio. After the accounts were closed, it was discovered that the following provisions of the deed had been ignored:
(i) Interest on capital at 10% p.a. was not allowed.
(ii) Interest on drawings was not charged: Pallavi ₹3,000, Qadir ₹2,000 and Rohan ₹1,000.
(iii) Qadir's salary of ₹12,000 for the year was not credited.
The partners decide to correct these omissions through their Current Accounts by a single adjusting entry, without reopening the old accounts.

Question: The total interest on capital that was omitted is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹60,000
Step 1: Pallavi = ₹3,00,000 × 10% = ₹30,000; Qadir = ₹2,00,000 × 10% = ₹20,000; Rohan = ₹1,00,000 × 10% = ₹10,000
Step 2: Total = ₹60,000
Common mistake: Taking 10% of the profit gives ₹18,000 (A). ₹30,000 (B) is Pallavi's interest only. ₹6,000 (C) is the total interest on drawings.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — net change in divisible profit
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Pallavi, Qadir and Rohan are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Their capitals are fixed at ₹3,00,000, ₹2,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. The firm's profit of ₹1,80,000 for 2025-26 was distributed among them in their profit-sharing ratio. After the accounts were closed, it was discovered that the following provisions of the deed had been ignored:
(i) Interest on capital at 10% p.a. was not allowed.
(ii) Interest on drawings was not charged: Pallavi ₹3,000, Qadir ₹2,000 and Rohan ₹1,000.
(iii) Qadir's salary of ₹12,000 for the year was not credited.
The partners decide to correct these omissions through their Current Accounts by a single adjusting entry, without reopening the old accounts.

Question: Taking all three omissions together, by how much was the profit distributed in the profit-sharing ratio overstated?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹66,000
Step 1: Items that should have reduced divisible profit: interest on capital ₹60,000 + salary ₹12,000 = ₹72,000
Step 2: Item that should have increased it: interest on drawings ₹6,000
Step 3: Net overstatement = ₹72,000 − ₹6,000 = ₹66,000
Common mistake: Adding the interest on drawings gives ₹78,000 (B). Ignoring it gives ₹72,000 (C). Ignoring the salary gives ₹54,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — net effect on one partner
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Pallavi, Qadir and Rohan are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Their capitals are fixed at ₹3,00,000, ₹2,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. The firm's profit of ₹1,80,000 for 2025-26 was distributed among them in their profit-sharing ratio. After the accounts were closed, it was discovered that the following provisions of the deed had been ignored:
(i) Interest on capital at 10% p.a. was not allowed.
(ii) Interest on drawings was not charged: Pallavi ₹3,000, Qadir ₹2,000 and Rohan ₹1,000.
(iii) Qadir's salary of ₹12,000 for the year was not credited.
The partners decide to correct these omissions through their Current Accounts by a single adjusting entry, without reopening the old accounts.

Question: The net effect of the omissions on Pallavi's Current Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Debit ₹6,000
Step 1: Interest on capital to be credited = +₹30,000
Step 2: Interest on drawings to be debited = −₹3,000
Step 3: Excess profit to be withdrawn (3/6 of ₹66,000) = −₹33,000
Step 4: Net = 30,000 − 3,000 − 33,000 = −₹6,000 → debit
Common mistake: Reversing the sign gives (A). Forgetting the interest on drawings gives ₹3,000 (B). ₹33,000 (D) is only the profit withdrawn.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — single adjusting entry for three partners
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Pallavi, Qadir and Rohan are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Their capitals are fixed at ₹3,00,000, ₹2,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. The firm's profit of ₹1,80,000 for 2025-26 was distributed among them in their profit-sharing ratio. After the accounts were closed, it was discovered that the following provisions of the deed had been ignored:
(i) Interest on capital at 10% p.a. was not allowed.
(ii) Interest on drawings was not charged: Pallavi ₹3,000, Qadir ₹2,000 and Rohan ₹1,000.
(iii) Qadir's salary of ₹12,000 for the year was not credited.
The partners decide to correct these omissions through their Current Accounts by a single adjusting entry, without reopening the old accounts.

Question: The single adjusting entry to correct the omissions is:
options: A) Qadir's Current A/c Dr. ₹8,000; To Pallavi's Current A/c ₹6,000; To Rohan's Current A/c ₹2,000
B) Pallavi's Current A/c Dr. ₹6,000; Rohan's Current A/c Dr. ₹2,000; To Qadir's Current A/c ₹8,000
C) Pallavi's Current A/c Dr. ₹6,000; To Qadir's Current A/c ₹6,000
D) Pallavi's Current A/c Dr. ₹4,000; Rohan's Current A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To Qadir's Current A/c ₹8,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Pallavi's Current A/c Dr. ₹6,000; Rohan's Current A/c Dr. ₹2,000; To Qadir's Current A/c ₹8,000
Step 1: Excess profit ₹66,000 withdrawn 3 : 2 : 1 → Pallavi ₹33,000; Qadir ₹22,000; Rohan ₹11,000
Step 2: Pallavi = +30,000 − 3,000 − 33,000 = −₹6,000
Step 3: Qadir = +20,000 − 2,000 + 12,000 − 22,000 = +₹8,000
Step 4: Rohan = +10,000 − 1,000 − 11,000 = −₹2,000 (net total = 0 ✔)
Common mistake: Reversing the debits and credits gives (A). Forgetting Rohan gives (C). Splitting Qadir's credit equally gives (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — an additional wrong credit
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Pallavi, Qadir and Rohan are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Their capitals are fixed at ₹3,00,000, ₹2,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. The firm's profit of ₹1,80,000 for 2025-26 was distributed among them in their profit-sharing ratio. After the accounts were closed, it was discovered that the following provisions of the deed had been ignored:
(i) Interest on capital at 10% p.a. was not allowed.
(ii) Interest on drawings was not charged: Pallavi ₹3,000, Qadir ₹2,000 and Rohan ₹1,000.
(iii) Qadir's salary of ₹12,000 for the year was not credited.
The partners decide to correct these omissions through their Current Accounts by a single adjusting entry, without reopening the old accounts.

Question: Suppose it is ALSO discovered that Rohan had been wrongly credited with a commission of ₹6,000 to which he was not entitled. After including this, the total amount debited to Rohan in the adjusting entry would be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹7,000
Step 1: Reversing the commission: Rohan −₹6,000
Step 2: The commission had reduced divisible profit, so profit rises by ₹6,000; Rohan's share (1/6) = +₹1,000
Step 3: Rohan's net = −2,000 (original omissions) − 6,000 + 1,000 = −₹7,000 → debit ₹7,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the profit-share effect gives ₹8,000 (A). ₹2,000 (B) ignores the commission. ₹6,000 (C) considers only the commission.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Activity ratios — trade payables turnover
questions.question: Net credit purchases for the year are ₹4,80,000. Trade payables were ₹50,000 at the beginning and ₹70,000 at the end of the year. The trade payables turnover ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 8 times
Step 1: Average trade payables = (₹50,000 + ₹70,000) ÷ 2 = ₹60,000
Step 2: Turnover = ₹4,80,000 ÷ ₹60,000 = 8 times (average payment period = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 months)
Common mistake: Using the closing payables gives 6.86 times (A). Using the opening payables gives 9.6 times (C). 1.5 (D) is the payment period in months, not the ratio.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Activity ratios — inventory turnover with carriage inwards
questions.question: Opening inventory was ₹40,000, purchases ₹3,20,000, carriage inwards ₹20,000 and closing inventory ₹60,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 6.4 times
Step 1: Cost of revenue from operations = Opening inventory + Purchases + Carriage inwards − Closing inventory = 40,000 + 3,20,000 + 20,000 − 60,000 = ₹3,20,000
Step 2: Average inventory = (₹40,000 + ₹60,000) ÷ 2 = ₹50,000
Step 3: Inventory turnover = ₹3,20,000 ÷ ₹50,000 = 6.4 times
Common mistake: Leaving out carriage inwards (a direct expense) gives 6 times (B). Using the closing inventory gives 5.33 times (C). Using the opening inventory gives 8 times (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Current ratio after credit purchase and payment
questions.question: A company has current assets of ₹3,00,000 and current liabilities of ₹1,50,000. It then (i) buys goods on credit for ₹50,000 and (ii) pays creditors ₹30,000 in cash. Its current ratio after both transactions is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1.88 : 1
Step 1: After (i): CA = ₹3,50,000; CL = ₹2,00,000
Step 2: After (ii): CA = ₹3,20,000; CL = ₹1,70,000
Step 3: Current ratio = ₹3,20,000 ÷ ₹1,70,000 = 1.88 : 1
Common mistake: Assuming no change gives 2 : 1 (A). Recording only (i) gives 1.75 : 1 (B). Changing only the current assets gives 2.13 : 1 (C).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Objectives and limitations of financial analysis
questions.question:
Which of the following are objectives of the analysis of financial statements?
(A) To assess the earning capacity of the business
(B) To assess its short-term and long-term solvency
(C) To make inter-firm comparisons
(D) To remove the effect of changes in the price level
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Analysis helps judge profitability (A), solvency (B), and performance compared with other firms (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — financial statements are based on historical cost, and their analysis does NOT remove price-level effects; ignoring price-level changes is a LIMITATION of analysis. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Analysis interprets historical figures; it cannot correct them for inflation.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from operating activities — adjustments
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II for calculating cash flow from operating activities by the indirect method:

List-I (Item)
(A) Depreciation
(B) Increase in inventories
(C) Profit on sale of machinery
(D) Increase in outstanding expenses

List-II (Treatment)
(I) Added back, as a non-cash expense
(II) Deducted, as an increase in a current asset
(III) Deducted, as a non-operating gain (the sale proceeds are shown under investing activities)
(IV) Added, as an increase in a current liability
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Depreciation reduced profit without any cash outflow → added back (I).
(B) More inventory ties up cash → deducted (II).
(C) The profit on sale is not an operating cash flow → deducted (III).
(D) Expenses not yet paid conserve cash → added (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps depreciation and outstanding expenses; (C) swaps inventories and profit on sale; (D) swaps depreciation and inventories.
Key point: Current assets up → deduct; current liabilities up → add.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Return on investment — formula
questions.question: Return on investment (return on capital employed) is calculated as:
options: A) Profit before interest and tax ÷ Capital employed × 100
B) Profit after tax ÷ Revenue from operations × 100
D) Profit after tax ÷ Shareholders' funds × 100
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Profit before interest and tax ÷ Capital employed × 100
Why: ROI measures the return on ALL long-term funds (equity plus debt), so the profit used is before interest (the return to lenders) and before tax.
Why not the others:
(B) is the net profit ratio.
(C) uses the wrong profit.
(D) is the return on shareholders' funds only.
Key point: All long-term funds ↔ PBIT.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Schedule III — unpaid dividend
questions.question: Dividend declared but not yet claimed by shareholders (unpaid dividend) is shown in a company's balance sheet under:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Other current liabilities
Why: Once declared, the dividend is a definite amount owed to shareholders. Unclaimed or unpaid dividend therefore appears under Other current liabilities.
Why not the others:
(A) Provisions are for estimated amounts.
(B) Trade payables arise from purchases.
(D) Reserves are part of shareholders' funds, not liabilities.
Key point: Unpaid dividend, interest accrued and calls in advance → other current liabilities.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Profitability ratios — gross profit ratio net of sales returns
questions.question: Sona Ltd. made gross sales of ₹5,20,000, with sales returns of ₹20,000. Its cost of revenue from operations was ₹3,50,000. Its gross profit ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 30%
Step 1: Revenue from operations = ₹5,20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹5,00,000
Step 2: Gross profit = ₹5,00,000 − ₹3,50,000 = ₹1,50,000
Step 3: GP ratio = ₹1,50,000 ÷ ₹5,00,000 × 100 = 30%
Common mistake: Ignoring the returns altogether gives 32.7% (A). 70% (B) is the cost ratio. Deducting returns from cost instead of sales gives 34% (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Activity ratios — trade receivables turnover with cash sales and bills receivable
questions.question: Total revenue from operations of Vega Ltd. is ₹7,50,000, of which cash sales are 20%. Debtors were ₹70,000 at the start of the year and ₹1,10,000 at the end, and bills receivable were ₹10,000 at both dates. The trade receivables turnover ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 6 times
Step 1: Credit revenue = 80% × ₹7,50,000 = ₹6,00,000
Step 2: Trade receivables include bills receivable: opening ₹80,000; closing ₹1,20,000 → average ₹1,00,000
Step 3: Turnover = ₹6,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = 6 times
Common mistake: Using total revenue gives 7.5 times (B). Leaving out bills receivable (average ₹90,000) gives 6.67 times (C). Using the closing balance gives 5 times (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from investing activities — machinery purchased (working back)
questions.question: Machinery (net of depreciation) stood at ₹2,00,000 at the start of the year and ₹2,60,000 at the end. Depreciation charged for the year was ₹30,000, and a machine with a book value of ₹20,000 was sold during the year. The machinery purchased during the year, shown as an investing outflow, is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,10,000
Step 1: Closing = Opening + Purchases − Depreciation − Book value of machine sold
Step 2: ₹2,60,000 = ₹2,00,000 + Purchases − ₹30,000 − ₹20,000
Step 3: Purchases = 2,60,000 + 30,000 + 20,000 − 2,00,000 = ₹1,10,000
Common mistake: The simple difference in balances gives ₹60,000 (A). Ignoring the machine sold gives ₹90,000 (B). Ignoring depreciation gives ₹80,000 (D).
Key point: Rebuild the Machinery Account to find the missing purchase figure.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — error values
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Error value)
(A) #DIV/0!
(B) #NAME?
(C) #REF!
(D) #VALUE!

List-II (Cause)
(I) A number is divided by zero or by an empty cell
(II) The spreadsheet does not recognise a function name
(III) A formula refers to a cell that is no longer valid
(IV) An argument is of the wrong type, such as text where a number is needed
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) #DIV/0! → division by zero (I).
(B) #NAME? → a misspelt function, such as =SUMM( (II).
(C) #REF! → a deleted or invalid reference (III).
(D) #VALUE! → the wrong data type (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps DIV/0 and NAME; (B) swaps NAME and REF; (C) swaps DIV/0 and VALUE.
Key point: Reading the error value tells you what to fix.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Loan repayment schedule — principal in the first EMI
questions.question: A loan of ₹2,40,000 at 12% p.a. is repaid in equal monthly instalments (EMIs) of ₹10,000, with interest calculated monthly on the outstanding balance. In the loan schedule, the principal portion of the FIRST EMI is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹7,600
Step 1: Monthly rate = 12% ÷ 12 = 1%
Step 2: Interest in month 1 = ₹2,40,000 × 1% = ₹2,400
Step 3: Principal = EMI − Interest = ₹10,000 − ₹2,400 = ₹7,600
Common mistake: ₹10,000 (A) is the whole EMI. ₹2,400 (B) is the interest portion. Using 1.2% a month gives ₹7,120 (C).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Depreciation schedule — SLN for an asset bought mid-year
questions.question: A machine costing ₹1,20,000 (no salvage value, life 5 years) was bought on 1 October 2025. The depreciation schedule uses =SLN for the annual amount and charges depreciation for the period of use. The year ends on 31 March. Accumulated depreciation at 31 March 2027 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹36,000
Step 1: =SLN(120000,0,5) = ₹24,000 a year
Step 2: 2025-26 (6 months) = ₹24,000 × 6/12 = ₹12,000
Step 3: 2026-27 (full year) = ₹24,000
Step 4: Accumulated = ₹12,000 + ₹24,000 = ₹36,000
Common mistake: Two full years gives ₹48,000 (A). ₹24,000 (B) is one year. ₹12,000 (D) is only the first year's charge.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — COUNT versus COUNTA
questions.question: In an expense sheet, cells A1 to A5 contain 100, the text Rent, (blank), 250 and 0. The formula =COUNT(A1:A5) returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3
Why: COUNT counts only cells that contain numbers — 100, 250 and 0. A zero is a number, so it is counted; text and blanks are not.
Why not the others:
(A) 4 is what COUNTA returns (it counts every non-empty cell, including text).
(B) 2 wrongly leaves out the zero.
(D) 5 counts every cell, including the blank.
Key point: COUNT → numbers only; COUNTA → anything non-empty; COUNTBLANK → empty cells.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — entering a formula
questions.question: In a spreadsheet, a formula is entered by typing which character first?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) =
Why: The equal sign tells the spreadsheet that what follows is a formula to be calculated, for example =B2*12%.
Why not the others:
(A) # appears in error values.
(B) @ is not used to start formulas.
(C) $ makes a reference absolute.
Key point: Every formula starts with '='.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Preparing reports using pivot table — features
questions.question:
Which of the following statements about pivot tables are correct?
(A) They summarise large volumes of data quickly.
(B) When the source data changes, the pivot table updates automatically without being refreshed.
(C) Fields can be moved between rows and columns to change the view.
(D) Values can be summarised by sum, count or average.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: Pivot tables condense data (A), let the user rearrange fields to view it differently (C), and can summarise values in several ways (D).
Why not the others: Statement (B) is false — a pivot table must be REFRESHED to reflect changes in its source data. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Changed the data? Refresh the pivot.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll — IF function for DA at the boundary
questions.question: A payroll sheet calculates DA with =IF(C2>50000,C2*30%,C2*40%). An employee's basic pay in C2 is exactly ₹50,000. The DA calculated is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹20,000
Why: The test is strictly 'greater than' 50,000. Since 50,000 is not greater than 50,000, the condition is FALSE and the second rate applies: ₹50,000 × 40% = ₹20,000.
Why not the others:
(A) ₹15,000 wrongly treats the condition as true.
(C) ₹50,000 is the basic pay.
(D) ₹35,000 adds the two rates.
Key point: '>' excludes the boundary; '>=' includes it.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — ROUND with negative digits
questions.question: The formula =ROUND(2345.678,-2) returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2300
Why: A negative number of digits rounds to the LEFT of the decimal point; −2 rounds to the nearest hundred. 2345.678 is nearer 2300 than 2400.
Why not the others:
(B) 2345.68 is ROUND(…,2).
(C) 2400 would need ROUNDUP.
(D) 2346 is ROUND(…,0).
Key point: Positive digits → decimals; negative digits → tens, hundreds, thousands.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — data validation
questions.question: In a payroll sheet, the 'Days Present' column must accept only whole numbers from 0 to 31. The spreadsheet feature used to enforce this is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Data Validation
Why: Data Validation restricts what may be entered in a cell (type, range or list) and rejects invalid entries, which reduces input errors.
Why not the others:
(A) Conditional Formatting only changes how cells look.
(C) Sorting reorders data.
(D) Freeze Panes keeps headings visible while scrolling.
Key point: Validation controls input; formatting controls appearance.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — text and value functions combined
questions.question: Cell A2 contains the invoice number INV-2026-0457 as text. The formula =VALUE(MID(A2,5,4))+1 returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2027
Step 1: MID(A2,5,4) takes 4 characters starting at position 5: 'I-N-V-hyphen' are positions 1–4, so it returns the text "2026"
Step 2: VALUE turns the text "2026" into the number 2026
Step 3: 2026 + 1 = 2027
Common mistake: Joining the text with & instead of adding gives 20261 (B). Assuming text cannot be converted gives #VALUE! (C). Forgetting the +1 gives 2026 (D).
